To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
NF-kappaB-inhibition in AML cells induces HO-1, which protects the AML cells from undergoing apoptosis.

HO-1 is suppressed in AML cells, and that this suppression of HO1 in AML is controlled by the NF-kappa B pathway, thus providing a mechanism for the resistance of AML cells to tumor necrosis-induced apoptosis.
NF-kappaB-inhibited AML cells are rescued from TNF-induced apoptosis by heme-oxygenase-1 (HMOX1) induction.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms by which NF-kappaB regulates HO-1 in primary human AML cells.
the molecular mechanisms underlying the chemoresistance and survival of acute myeloid leukemic cells.
understanding how NF-kappaB and HO-1 interact in AML.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
NF-kappaB-inhibition induced HO-1 in a p50- and p65-dependent manner, which in turn protected AML from apoptosis.
the inhibition of NF-kB in AML cells results in the induction of HO-1, which in turn provides an anti-apoptotic mechanism to rescue the AML cells from apoptosis.
HO-1 induction is a mechanism of NF-kappa B-mediated resistance to apoptosis in acute myelogenous leukemia (AML) and is a potential therapeutic target for overcoming chemoresistance in AML.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
NF-kappaB inhibited AML cells are rescued from cell death by heme oxygenases-1 induction.
HO-1 is suppressed by NF-kappaB, and this suppression is important in the resistance of AML cells to chemotherapy.
NF-kappaB-inhibiting agents are not effective in AML because of a secondary mechanism that is induced by HO-1, which is a silent factor in AML.
The main takeaway from our work is that

HO-1 is not an antiapoptotic gene in normal cells, but in AML cells, it is a secondary antiapoptic gene that is only activated when NF-kappa B is suppressed, and thus provides an additional survival mechanism in AML cells.
NF-kappaB and HO-1 work together in AML cells, and that inhibiting both of these pathways is required to induce apoptosis in AML.
heme oxygen-ase-1 is a secondary survival pathway in acute myelogenous leukemia cells that becomes active only when the primary survival mechanism, nuclear factor-kappaB, is inhibited.
